It defines what tables exist, what columns they have, what data types, what constraints, what relationships. This is set at design time and rarely changes once the system is in production. Extension on the other hand refers to the actual data at a given moment — how many tuples are currently in each table. As users insert, update, or delete records, the extension changes constantly. So if you think of a student database — the intension is the fact that there's a Student table with columns student_id, name, and course — that doesn't change. The extension is the current set of student records, which changes every semester when new students enroll or old ones graduate.

Intension is the database schema — it defines the structure and is mostly fixed. Extension is the actual data at a given point in time — it changes as records are added or removed. Intension is like the structure, extension is like the content.
Intension is the design of the database and extension is the data inside it. Intension doesn't change much but extension changes all the time because data is being added and deleted.

Intension and extension are both ways to describe the database state. Intension refers to the current set of records in the database — it's a real-time count of how many tuples are present in each table. Extension refers to the schema definition that was specified when the database was first created. Extension is static and doesn't change, while intension is dynamic and updates whenever data is modified. Both together give a complete picture of the database at any point in time.
Intension means the database is intense — it has a lot of data. Extension means the database has been extended with new tables. They are used to measure how much the database has grown over time.

rubric.concept_name: Intension as database schema — static structure
rubric.reference_explanation: Intension, also known as database schema, is the description or definition of the database. It is specified during the design phase and mostly remains unchanged over the database's lifetime.

rubric.concept_name: Extension as database snapshot — dynamic data
rubric.reference_explanation: Extension is the measure of the number of tuples present in the database at any given point in time. It is also referred to as the snapshot of the database, and its value changes as tuples are created, updated, or deleted.

subject: Database Management Systems
question: Explain the difference between the DELETE and TRUNCATE command in a DBMS.

answers.text: DELETE and TRUNCATE both remove data, but they work very differently. DELETE is a DML command and it deletes specific rows based on a WHERE clause. So you can say DELETE FROM students WHERE grade = 'F' and only failing students get removed. It logs each row before deleting — that's why it can be rolled back but it's also slower. TRUNCATE is more nuclear — it wipes out all rows from a table in one shot with no WHERE clause. It doesn't log individual row deletions, so it's much faster, but there's less control. It's essentially a DDL command. One key difference is speed and rollback — DELETE is slower but rollback-safe at row level, TRUNCATE is fast but you're dropping everything at once. If you just need to clear a table quickly, TRUNCATE is the way to go. If you need precision, use DELETE.

DELETE removes specific rows using a WHERE clause and can be rolled back. It's slower because it logs each deletion. TRUNCATE removes all rows from a table at once and is faster because it doesn't log row by row. TRUNCATE doesn't use a WHERE clause.

DELETE is used to remove specific rows and TRUNCATE removes all data from a table. DELETE is slower and TRUNCATE is faster. DELETE uses WHERE clause but TRUNCATE doesn't. Both can be rolled back I think.

DELETE and TRUNCATE are both used to remove data from a database. DELETE is a DDL command that operates on the table structure itself — when you delete a table, the schema is also removed. TRUNCATE is a DML command that removes individual rows based on internal criteria. DELETE is faster because it removes the entire object in one step, while TRUNCATE goes row by row to selectively remove data. Both commands automatically commit after execution and cannot be rolled back.
DELETE and TRUNCATE are the same command with different syntax. DELETE removes a table from the database and TRUNCATE deletes individual columns. Both require the DROP privilege.

rubric.concept_name: DELETE — conditional row removal with logging
rubric.reference_explanation: DELETE removes rows from a table based on a WHERE clause condition. It maintains a log to lock rows before deleting, which makes it slower. It can be rolled back since it is a DML operation.

rubric.concept_name: TRUNCATE — complete table data removal without logging
rubric.reference_explanation: TRUNCATE removes all data from a table at once without a WHERE clause. It does not maintain a row-level log and operates on the whole table, making it faster than DELETE. It is a DDL operation.

DELETE can be rolled back because it is logged at the row level. TRUNCATE in most DBMS systems cannot be rolled back (though the PDF states it can, the standard behavior in most databases like MySQL is that TRUNCATE is not fully rollback-safe outside a transaction).

subject: Database Management Systems
question: What is a lock? Explain the major difference between a shared lock and an exclusive lock during a transaction in a database.

answers.text: A lock in a database is a mechanism used to manage concurrent access to data. When a transaction is working on a piece of data, a lock prevents other transactions from interfering with it. Without locks you'd have dirty reads, lost updates, all sorts of nasty concurrency problems. Now there are two main types. A shared lock is used when a transaction is reading data. Many transactions can hold a shared lock on the same item at the same time — they're all just reading, so they don't conflict. Think of it like many people reading the same document. An exclusive lock is used when a transaction wants to write — update or insert. Only one transaction can hold an exclusive lock, and while it does, no other transaction can read or write that data item. This ensures that writes are isolated. The distinction matters because shared locks maximize read throughput while exclusive locks ensure write consistency. A shared lock won't block another shared lock, but an exclusive lock blocks everything.

A lock protects data from being updated by multiple users at the same time. A shared lock allows multiple transactions to read the same data concurrently. An exclusive lock is used for write operations and allows only one transaction at a time, preventing inconsistency.

Locks are used in databases to control access to data. Shared locks are for reading — multiple transactions can read at the same time. Exclusive locks are for writing — only one transaction can write. Locks prevent issues when multiple users access the same data.

A database lock is a data structure stored alongside each table row to track which user last modified it. A shared lock is applied when two or more transactions try to write the same data at the same time — it merges their changes to prevent conflicts. An exclusive lock is used during read operations to ensure that the data read by a transaction is not changed by anyone else before the read is complete. Exclusive locks are less restrictive than shared locks because they only block write operations.

Locks are passwords set on tables to prevent unauthorized access. A shared lock means everyone has the same password and can all edit the data. An exclusive lock means only one person knows the password and others can't access the table at all.

rubric.concept_name: Database lock — mechanism to prevent concurrent write conflicts
rubric.reference_explanation: A database lock is a mechanism that protects shared data from being updated by two or more users simultaneously. Once a session acquires a lock, no other session can modify that data until the lock is released.

A shared lock is required for reading a data item. Multiple transactions can hold shared locks on the same data item simultaneously — all of them are allowed to read, but none can write while shared locks are active.

An exclusive lock is applied when a transaction is about to perform a write operation. Only one transaction can hold an exclusive lock on a data item at a time, preventing any other transaction from reading or writing to that item.

subject: Database Management Systems
question: What is meant by normalization and denormalization?

answers.text: Normalization is the process of organizing a database to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity. The basic idea is to split data across multiple related tables so the same piece of information isn't stored in more than one place. For example, instead of storing a student's address in every row of an orders table, you store it once in a Students table and reference it with a key. This reduces duplication and makes updates easier. There are formal levels to this — 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF — each with stricter conditions. Denormalization is kind of the opposite. Once data is normalized and split across many tables, querying it requires JOINs, which can be slow. Denormalization merges some of those tables back together to make reads faster, even though it reintroduces some redundancy. It's a tradeoff — normalized databases are better for write-heavy systems, denormalized are better for read-heavy analytics.

Normalization splits data into multiple tables to reduce redundancy and improve integrity. Denormalization combines those tables back into one to make data retrieval faster. JOIN operations can create denormalized data. It's a tradeoff between write efficiency and read speed.

Normalization is about reducing duplicate data by organizing it into tables. Denormalization is the opposite — it merges tables to speed up queries. Normalization is good for storage and denormalization is good for reading data quickly.

Normalization and denormalization are two strategies for database performance tuning. Normalization increases redundancy by creating copies of data across multiple tables, which allows parallel reads and improves read performance. Denormalization reduces the number of tables by deleting redundant records, which reduces storage and improves write performance. The normal forms like 1NF and 2NF are standards that guide how much normalization should be applied based on query workload.

Normalization means the database follows normal standards and conventions. Denormalization means the database was customized and is no longer standard. Normalized databases are slower than denormalized ones in all scenarios.

rubric.concept_name: Normalization — reducing redundancy through table decomposition
rubric.reference_explanation: Normalization is the process of reducing redundancy by organizing data into multiple tables. It leads to better disk space usage and makes it easier to maintain database integrity.

rubric.concept_name: Denormalization — combining tables for faster retrieval
rubric.reference_explanation: Denormalization is the reverse process of normalization. It combines normalized tables back into fewer tables to make data retrieval faster, at the cost of increased redundancy. JOIN operations can be used to create denormalized forms.

subject: Database Management Systems
question: Explain different types of Normalization forms in a DBMS.

answers.text: There are four main normal forms. 1NF — First Normal Form — is the most basic. It requires that every column holds a single atomic value. No multiple values in one column, no repeating column groups, and each row must be uniquely identifiable. 2NF builds on 1NF and deals with partial dependencies. If the primary key is composite, every non-key attribute must depend on the whole key, not just part of it. So if you have a table keyed by (StudentID, CourseID), an attribute like StudentName depends only on StudentID — that's a partial dependency, and it violates 2NF. You'd separate it into different tables. 3NF eliminates transitive dependencies. Even if all non-key attributes depend on the full key, they shouldn't depend on each other. If A -> B and B -> C, then A -> C is a transitive dependency, which is not allowed in 3NF. BCNF or Boyce-Codd Normal Form is stricter than 3NF. The rule is: for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a super key. This handles edge cases that 3NF misses when there are multiple overlapping candidate keys.

1NF requires atomic values in each column and no duplicate columns. 2NF requires being in 1NF and no partial dependencies — all non-key attributes must depend on the whole primary key. 3NF requires being in 2NF and no transitive dependencies between non-key attributes. BCNF is stricter than 3NF — every determinant in a functional dependency must be a super key.

There are four normal forms. 1NF means each column should have one value. 2NF means no partial dependencies on the key. 3NF means no transitive dependencies. BCNF is like 3NF but stricter. Each form requires meeting the previous one first.

Normalization forms are levels of database optimization. 1NF means each table must have exactly one primary key — no table without a primary key can be in 1NF. 2NF means the table must have two or more columns, because a single-column table is considered flat. 3NF means the table must have been split into at least three separate tables to eliminate all redundancy. BCNF or Boyce-Codd Normal Form means every column in the table must have a unique index to ensure fast lookup and uniqueness, which is a stricter form of 3NF.

Normal forms are SQL commands used to format output. 1NF formats the output in one column, 2NF in two columns, and 3NF in three. BCNF means the output is in Boyce-Codd format which is the default for most databases.

rubric.reference_explanation: First Normal Form requires that every column has a single atomic value, duplicate columns from the same table are removed, and each row is identified with a unique column. Multi-valued attributes are not allowed.

rubric.concept_name: 2NF — full functional dependency on primary key
rubric.reference_explanation: Second Normal Form requires the table to be in 1NF and every non-prime attribute must be fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key, not just part of it. Partial dependencies must be eliminated.
Third Normal Form requires the table to be in 2NF and eliminates transitive functional dependencies — no non-prime attribute should depend on another non-prime attribute.

rubric.concept_name: BCNF — super key requirement for all determinants
rubric.reference_explanation: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (3.5NF) is a stricter form of 3NF. For every functional dependency A -> B, A must be a super key of the table. A non-prime attribute cannot be a determinant of a prime attribute.

subject: Database Management Systems
question: Explain different types of keys in a database.

answers.text: There are seven types of keys in a database. Candidate key — any attribute or set of attributes that can uniquely identify a row. A table can have multiple. Primary key — the candidate key we choose as the official identifier. It can't be NULL. Super key — any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row, including ones with extra unnecessary columns. Candidate keys are minimal super keys. Unique key — similar to primary key but allows NULLs. Alternate key — any candidate key that wasn't selected as the primary key. Foreign key — an attribute in one table that references the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity. For example, courseId in a Student table referencing a Course table. Composite key — a combination of two or more columns used together to uniquely identify a row. Each type has a specific purpose and together they define how data is identified, linked, and constrained across the database.

The main keys are primary, foreign, candidate, super, unique, alternate, and composite. Primary key uniquely identifies rows and doesn't allow NULLs. Foreign key links to another table's primary key. Candidate key is any minimal unique identifier. Super key includes candidate keys plus extra attributes. Unique key is like primary but allows NULLs. Alternate keys are candidate keys not used as primary. Composite key is made of multiple columns.

There are different keys in a database. Primary key uniquely identifies each row. Foreign key connects two tables. Candidate key is like a potential primary key. I think there's also a composite key which uses multiple columns. Not sure about all the others.

There are seven types of keys. The primary key is the most important and must contain unique values — it is automatically indexed by the DBMS. A candidate key is a key that is currently not active but can be promoted to primary key when needed, like a backup key. A super key is a special type of foreign key that links a child table back to a parent table in a self-referencing relationship. An alternate key is used when the primary key is unavailable due to NULL values — it serves as a replacement key. A composite key is any key that spans multiple tables. A unique key enforces uniqueness but also creates a clustered index on the column, unlike a primary key which uses a non-clustered index.

There is only one type of key in a database — the primary key. It is used to sort the table. Foreign key is not really a key, it's just a relationship. Candidate keys are used in NoSQL databases only.

rubric.reference_explanation: A candidate key is a set of attributes that can uniquely identify every tuple in a table. A table may have multiple candidate keys, and one of them is chosen as the primary key.

rubric.concept_name: Primary Key — chosen unique identifier with no NULLs
rubric.reference_explanation: A primary key is the candidate key chosen to uniquely identify every tuple. It does not allow NULL values and uniquely identifies each row in the table.

rubric.concept_name: Super Key — superset of candidate and primary keys
rubric.reference_explanation: A super key is any set of attributes that can uniquely identify a tuple. Candidate keys and primary keys are subsets of the super key — the super key may include redundant attributes.

rubric.concept_name: Foreign Key — referential link between tables
rubric.reference_explanation: A foreign key is an attribute in one table that can only take values present in the primary key column of another table, establishing a referential link between the two tables.

Unique key is like a primary key but allows NULL values. Alternate keys are candidate keys not chosen as the primary key. A composite key is a combination of two or more columns that together uniquely identify each tuple.

subject: Database Management Systems
question: Explain the difference between a 2-tier and 3-tier architecture in a DBMS.

answers.text: In 2-tier architecture, the client application communicates directly with the database server. There's no middleman — the application code and database are the two tiers. This is simple to set up and works fine for small systems, like a contact management system in MS-Access. But it has problems — if the business logic is on the client, every client needs to be updated when logic changes, and the database is directly exposed to the client which is a security concern. 3-tier architecture adds a middle layer — usually an application server. The client talks to the application server, which handles business logic and then queries the database. This is how most modern web applications work — browser is client, web server is the middle tier, database is the backend. The benefits are clear: better security since the DB is never directly exposed, easier to scale each layer independently, and logic changes are made on the server, not on every client.

2-tier is client-server architecture where the client directly communicates with the database. No middleware is involved. 3-tier adds a middle application layer between client and database, which improves security and scalability. In 3-tier, the client talks to the app server which then queries the database.

2-tier means there are two layers — the user and the database. The user connects directly to the database. 3-tier adds another layer in between, like a web server. 3-tier is more secure because the user doesn't directly access the database.

2-tier and 3-tier differ in how many databases they use. 2-tier uses a single database while 3-tier uses two databases — one for the application and one for backup. In 2-tier, the client and server communicate over HTTP while in 3-tier, they use a proprietary protocol defined by the DBMS. 3-tier is slower than 2-tier because of the extra round trip to the second database, but it provides redundancy. Both architectures require the client to have direct SQL access to at least one database.

2-tier means the application has two tables and 3-tier means it has three tables. More tiers means more data can be stored. The tier number refers to how many normalization levels were applied to the database design.

rubric.reference_explanation: In 2-tier architecture, the client application communicates directly with the database server with no middleware in between. The application logic resides on the client side. Examples include MS-Access-based systems or Railway Reservation systems.

In 3-tier architecture, there is an additional application/middleware layer between the client and the database server. The client interacts with the application server, which in turn communicates with the database. This improves security, scalability, and accessibility.

rubric.concept_name: Security and scalability differences between tiers
rubric.reference_explanation: 3-tier architecture is more secure because the client never directly accesses the database. The middleware layer also provides GUI and abstracts database logic, making the system more maintainable and scalable than 2-tier.

subject: Data Structures
question: What are Data Structures?

answers.text: A data structure is basically how you organize data inside a program so you can use it efficiently. Like, if you just dump all your data randomly, your program is gonna be slow and hard to manage. Different structures like arrays, linked lists, trees, and graphs exist because different problems need different ways of organizing things. The structure you pick determines how fast you can search, insert, or delete data.

Data structures are ways to store and organize data in memory. Things like arrays, stacks, queues are all data structures. The main point is that using the right one makes your program run better. Without them the computer wouldn't know how to handle data properly.

I think data structures are like containers that hold data. Arrays hold a bunch of numbers, linked lists hold nodes with pointers. They help organize data I guess. Not sure exactly how they affect performance but I know they're important in programming.

Data structures are programming constructs that define how data is displayed to the user. They are mainly used to improve the visual representation of information in applications. For example, a tree structure is used to show folder hierarchies on screen, and arrays are used for displaying lists in UI components.
Data structures are the syntax rules of a programming language that tell the computer how to read code. Every language has its own data structures which is why Python code doesn't work in Java.

rubric.reference_explanation: A data structure is a way of organizing and storing data in a computer so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently. It defines both the data and the operations that can be performed on it.
The choice of data structure directly affects the efficiency and performance of a program. Poor data organization leads to slower and less efficient code.
Common examples include arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, and graphs, each suited for different types of problems.

subject: Data Structures
question: Why Create Data Structures?

answers.text: The whole point of data structures is to make programs faster and easier to manage. If you're searching through a million records, the structure you use — like a hash map versus a plain array — makes a massive difference in how long it takes. They also make code cleaner because you're not just throwing data around randomly. And different problems genuinely need different approaches, like you wouldn't use an array when you need fast key-value lookups.

We create data structures to organize data so programs run efficiently. They help with things like searching and inserting data faster. They also make code easier to read and maintain. Without them programs would be slower and harder to manage.

Data structures help organize data I think. They make programs work better somehow. Like arrays help store things in order and linked lists help when you need to add things. I'm not totally sure about all the reasons but efficiency is one of them.

Data structures are created primarily to reduce the amount of memory a program uses. By choosing the right data structure, you can compress data more efficiently and avoid memory leaks. For instance, using a linked list instead of an array always saves memory because linked lists only allocate space as needed.
Data structures are created because programming languages require them to compile code. Without defining a data structure the compiler cannot understand what type of variable you are declaring.

rubric.reference_explanation: Data structures ensure that operations like search, insertion, and deletion are performed efficiently, reducing time and space complexity.
Data structures provide a clear organization to code, making it easier to understand, maintain, and debug.
Different problems require different data organizations. Data structures allow developers to choose the most appropriate structure for the problem at hand.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is a stack data structure? What are the applications of stack?

answers.text: A stack is a linear data structure where you can only add or remove from one end — the top. It works on LIFO, which means the last thing you put in is the first thing you take out, kind of like a stack of plates. The two main operations are push (add to top) and pop (remove from top). You see stacks everywhere — when your browser lets you hit the back button, that's a stack of visited pages. Also function calls use a call stack, and expression evaluation like converting infix to postfix uses stacks too.

A stack follows LIFO — last in first out. You push things onto the top and pop them off the top. Its used in undo operations in text editors, and also for function calls where the program keeps track of which function called which. Parenthesis matching also uses a stack.

A stack is a data structure where you add and remove from the same end. I think it's LIFO. Push adds something, pop removes it. It's used in some editor operations I believe. Not totally sure about all the applications.

A stack is a data structure based on the LIFO principle. It has push and pop operations. Because it processes the last inserted element first, stacks are ideal for sorting algorithms since you can always access the largest or smallest element at the top. This is why stacks are commonly used in database indexing to keep records sorted.
A stack is like an array but you can only access it from both ends. It uses FIFO so the first thing you put in comes out first. It's used in networking to send data packets in order.

rubric.reference_explanation: A stack follows the Last In First Out (LIFO) principle, meaning the last element added is the first one to be removed.
The two primary operations of a stack are push (adding an element to the top) and pop (removing the element from the top).
Stacks are used in undo/redo operations in editors, function call management (call stack), expression evaluation (infix to postfix), parenthesis matching, and backtracking algorithms.

subject: Data Structures
question: What are different operations available in stack data structure?

answers.text: The main stack operations are push, pop, peek, isEmpty, and size. Push adds to the top — if you push when full you get a stack overflow. Pop removes from the top — if you pop an empty stack you get underflow. Peek just lets you look at the top element without removing it, which is handy when you need to check what's there. isEmpty tells you if there's anything in the stack, and size gives you the count. Pretty simple set of operations but they're enough for everything stacks are used for.

Stack operations include push which adds an element to the top, pop which removes the top element, and peek which shows you the top without removing it. There's also isEmpty to check if the stack is empty. Overflow happens when you push to a full stack and underflow when you pop from an empty one.

Stack has push and pop I know that for sure. Push adds something, pop removes it. I think there's also a way to check if it's empty. Not sure if there are other operations. Overflow happens when the stack is too big I think.

Stack operations are push, pop, and peek. Push adds an element to the bottom of the stack to maintain the LIFO order, while pop retrieves the most recently added item from the top. Peek also removes the element but returns its value before deletion, which is useful for checking before removal.
Stack operations are enqueue and dequeue. Enqueue adds something to the back and dequeue removes from the front. This is what makes the stack a FIFO structure.

rubric.reference_explanation: Push adds an element to the top of the stack. If the stack is full, an overflow condition occurs.
Pop removes the top element from the stack. If the stack is empty, an underflow condition occurs.
The peek or top operation returns the top element of the stack without removing it.
isEmpty returns true if the stack contains no elements. Size returns the total number of elements currently in the stack.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is a queue data structure? What are the applications of queue?

answers.text: A queue is basically a line — first person in is first person out, that's FIFO. You add to the rear (enqueue) and remove from the front (dequeue). Real life example is literally any queue — people waiting at a ticket counter. In computing, OS uses queues for CPU scheduling, disk scheduling. BFS graph traversal also uses a queue because you need to process nodes level by level in the order you discovered them.

Queue is a FIFO data structure. Elements are added at the rear end and removed from the front. It's used in operating systems for scheduling tasks like CPU scheduling. Also used in BFS algorithm for graph traversal.
Queue works like a line of people, first in first out. You add to one end and remove from the other. I think it's used in scheduling somehow but I'm not sure exactly how. BFS might use it too.

A queue is a FIFO data structure where elements enter from the rear and exit from the front. Because it always processes in insertion order, queues are ideal for recursive algorithms that need to backtrack through previous states. This is why depth-first search uses a queue to explore all possible paths systematically.
A queue is like a stack but in reverse. It uses LIFO so the last thing added is the first removed. It's used to store variables in a program during compilation.

rubric.reference_explanation: A queue follows the First In First Out (FIFO) principle — the first element added is the first one to be removed, similar to a real-world queue of people.
Enqueue adds an element to the rear of the queue. Dequeue removes an element from the front of the queue.
Queues are used in CPU and disk scheduling in operating systems, breadth-first search in graphs, call center management systems, and printer spooling.

subject: Data Structures
question: Differentiate between stack and queue data structure.

answers.text: The biggest difference is how they handle order. Stack is LIFO — last in first out — so both adding and removing happen at the top. Queue is FIFO — first in first out — where you add at the rear and remove from the front. Because of this, stack only needs one pointer (top) while queue needs two (front and rear). Use cases differ too — stacks are great for recursion and backtracking, queues are better for scheduling and sequential processing like BFS.

Stack is LIFO and queue is FIFO. In a stack you push and pop from the same end. In a queue you enqueue at the back and dequeue from the front. Stacks use one pointer, queues use two. Stacks are used in recursion problems and queues in scheduling.
Stack is LIFO and queue is FIFO I know that. Stack operations happen at one end, queue uses two ends I think. Not sure about the pointers. They're used in different situations.

The main difference is that a stack uses LIFO while a queue uses FIFO. In terms of implementation, both structures use a single pointer — the stack uses 'top' and the queue uses 'front'. Queues have a rear pointer too but it only exists to optimize insertion speed, not as a structural requirement. Both are used interchangeably in most graph traversal algorithms.

Stack and queue are the same thing just with different names. Both remove elements from the front and that's the main idea behind both structures. The difference is just in programming language syntax.

rubric.reference_explanation: Stack uses LIFO (Last In First Out) while queue uses FIFO (First In First Out). This is the fundamental difference between the two.
In a stack, both insertion and deletion happen at the same end (top). In a queue, insertion happens at the rear and deletion happens at the front.
Stack uses a single pointer (top) for both operations. Queue uses two pointers — front for deletion and rear for insertion.
Stacks are suited for problems involving recursion and backtracking. Queues are suited for sequential processing and scheduling problems.

subject: Data Structures
question: How to implement a queue using stack?

answers.text: You need two stacks to pull this off. There are two ways to do it. First way: make enqueue expensive — when you enqueue, move everything from stack1 to stack2, push the new item to stack1, then move everything back. That way the oldest item is always at the top of stack1, so dequeue is O(1). Second way: make dequeue expensive — enqueue just pushes to stack1, which is O(1). But when you dequeue and stack2 is empty, you dump all of stack1 into stack2 and pop from there. This is better in practice because dequeue becomes amortized O(1).

You use two stacks. One way is to make enqueue costly by moving elements between the stacks each time you add so the oldest is always accessible first. The other way is to make dequeue costly — just push normally, but when dequeuing move everything to the second stack. Both approaches simulate FIFO behavior.

I think you can use two stacks to make a queue. Something about moving elements from one stack to another to reverse the order. That way you can get FIFO behavior. Not totally sure about the exact steps though.

To implement a queue using stacks, you use two stacks and reverse the LIFO order. During enqueue you push to stack1 normally. During dequeue you move all elements to stack2 and pop. The key insight is that after popping you must move all elements back to stack1 to maintain the correct order for future operations. This ensures both operations are O(n).
You can't really implement a queue using a stack because they work in opposite ways. A stack is LIFO and queue is FIFO so they are incompatible. You would need to use an array instead.

rubric.reference_explanation: A queue can be implemented using two stacks. Elements are moved between the stacks to simulate FIFO behavior using LIFO stacks.
In the costly enqueue approach, during enqueue, all elements are moved from stack1 to stack2, the new element is pushed to stack1, then everything is moved back. Dequeue is O(1).

In the costly dequeue approach, enqueue simply pushes to stack1 (O(1)). During dequeue, if stack2 is empty, all elements from stack1 are moved to stack2 and the top is popped. This achieves amortized O(1) dequeue.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is array data structure? What are the applications of arrays?

answers.text: An array is a collection of same-type elements stored in contiguous memory. What makes it powerful is index-based access — you can get any element in O(1) because the address is just base address plus offset. The downside is the fixed size — you declare how big it is upfront and that's it. Applications are everywhere: implementing stacks and queues, storing matrix data, image processing where each pixel is stored in a 2D array, and it's the foundation for basically all sorting algorithms.

Arrays store elements of the same type in contiguous memory. You access elements using an index which makes it really fast — O(1) access. Size is fixed though so you can't grow it. Used in implementing stacks, queues, and for storing matrices.
An array is a bunch of elements stored together. You can access them with an index. I think the size is fixed when you create it. It's used in a lot of programs for storing data.

An array stores elements of the same type in contiguous memory. Because all elements are adjacent in memory, inserting a new element in the middle is very efficient since you just place it in the next available slot. This is why arrays are preferred over linked lists for insertion-heavy applications like real-time data feeds.

An array is a data structure that stores different types of data together. You can store integers, strings, and objects all in one array. The size changes automatically as you add more elements so you never run out of space.

rubric.reference_explanation: An array is a collection of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous memory locations, accessible via an index.
Arrays provide O(1) random access to any element using its index, making retrieval very fast.
The size of an array is typically fixed at declaration and cannot be changed at runtime in most implementations.
Arrays are used in implementing other data structures (stacks, queues), storing matrices, database records, image pixel data, and as a foundation for sorting and searching algorithms.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is a linked list data structure? What are the applications for the Linked list?

answers.text: A linked list is made up of nodes, where each node has two parts — the data and a pointer to the next node. The nodes don't have to be in contiguous memory, which is the main difference from arrays. The big advantage is that it's dynamic — you can add or remove nodes without worrying about a fixed size. Downside is accessing an element takes O(n) since you have to traverse from the head. Used in implementing stacks, queues, OS memory management, and browser history navigation.

A linked list has nodes with data and a pointer to the next node. Memory isn't contiguous. You can grow it dynamically which is better than arrays in that sense. Used in stacks, queues, and OS memory management.
Linked list has nodes connected together. Each node points to the next one. It's dynamic so you can add more nodes. Not sure about all the applications but I think it's used in some OS stuff.

A linked list is a dynamic data structure where each node stores data and a pointer to the next node. Because nodes are stored in contiguous memory, traversal is very fast — O(1) — since the CPU can predict the next memory address. This is why linked lists are faster than arrays for sequential access operations.

A linked list is just like an array but with a different name. Elements are stored in index positions and you access them the same way with brackets like list[0]. The only difference is it uses more memory.

rubric.reference_explanation: A linked list consists of nodes where each node contains a data field and a pointer (or reference) to the next node in the sequence.
Unlike arrays, linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically at runtime by allocating or deallocating memory as needed.
Linked list nodes are stored at random memory locations and connected through pointers, unlike arrays which require contiguous memory.
Linked lists are used to implement stacks, queues, graphs, dynamic memory allocation in OS, browser forward/backward navigation, and music playlist management.

subject: Data Structures
question: Difference between Array and Linked List.

answers.text: Arrays and linked lists differ in a few key ways. Memory: arrays need contiguous block, linked lists scatter nodes anywhere in memory. Access: arrays are O(1) with index, linked lists are O(n) because you traverse. Insertion/deletion: arrays require shifting elements so it's O(n), but linked lists can do it in O(1) if you already have the position. Memory-wise, linked lists have overhead from storing pointers, while arrays might waste space if they're not full. So basically — use arrays when you need fast access, linked lists when you're doing lots of insertions and deletions.

Arrays use contiguous memory and linked lists don't. Arrays have O(1) access, linked lists O(n). Insertion is faster in linked lists. Arrays have fixed size, linked lists are dynamic. Linked lists use more memory per element because of pointers.

Arrays and linked lists are different. Arrays need contiguous memory. Linked lists are more flexible. I think arrays are faster to access but linked lists are easier to modify. Memory is also different somehow.

The main difference between arrays and linked lists is memory layout. Arrays use contiguous memory so cache performance is worse, while linked lists store nodes anywhere in memory so the CPU cache can fetch them much more efficiently. This makes linked lists faster for read-heavy applications where you frequently access many elements.
Arrays and linked lists are the same. Both store data in sequential order and have O(1) access time. Linked lists are just a newer version of arrays with extra features added.

rubric.reference_explanation: Arrays use contiguous memory allocation with fixed size. Linked lists use dynamic, non-contiguous memory allocation.
Arrays provide O(1) random access via index. Linked lists require O(n) sequential traversal to access elements.
Insertion and deletion in arrays is O(n) due to shifting. In linked lists, these are O(1) if the position is known, making linked lists better for frequent modifications.
Linked lists require extra memory for storing pointers in each node. Arrays have no such overhead but may waste memory if not fully utilized.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is an asymptotic analysis of an algorithm?

answers.text: Asymptotic analysis is how we measure algorithm performance mathematically without worrying about hardware or implementation details. We look at how the runtime scales as input size grows to infinity. There are three main notations: Big O gives the worst case — if you search linearly through n elements in the worst case you look at all n, so O(n). Omega gives the best case — linear search finds it on the first try in Omega(1). Theta gives the tight bound when best and worst are the same asymptotically. This helps us compare algorithms in a machine-independent way.

Asymptotic analysis evaluates algorithm performance as input grows. Big O is worst case, Omega is best case, Theta is average. It helps compare algorithms independently of hardware. Most of the time we care about Big O in practice.
Asymptotic analysis is about how fast an algorithm runs. Big O is the main one I know, it's the worst case. I think Omega is best case. Not sure what Theta is exactly. It helps measure efficiency.

Asymptotic analysis measures how efficiently an algorithm runs by counting the exact number of operations it performs. Big O notation gives the precise operation count, so O(n) means exactly n operations. Omega notation gives the minimum guaranteed operations, and Theta gives the most common number of operations across all inputs.
Asymptotic analysis is a tool used to measure how much RAM an algorithm uses. O(n) means the algorithm uses n megabytes of memory. If an algorithm is O(1) it means it uses no memory at all.

rubric.reference_explanation: Asymptotic analysis is a method of describing the runtime or space behavior of an algorithm as the input size grows toward infinity, expressed using mathematical notations.
Big O notation (O) describes the upper bound or worst-case time complexity of an algorithm — the maximum time it could take.
Omega notation (Ω) describes the lower bound or best-case time complexity — the minimum time an algorithm will take.
Theta notation (θ) describes the tight bound — the average-case complexity when the algorithm's runtime is bounded both above and below by the same function.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is hashmap in data structure?

answers.text: A hashmap stores data as key-value pairs using a hash table under the hood. You give it a key, the hash function converts that key into an array index, and the value is stored there. That's why retrieval is O(1) on average — you just compute the hash and go directly to that index. It's like having a dictionary where looking up any word takes the same time no matter how many words are in it. Very useful when you need fast lookups.
A hashmap stores key-value pairs and uses hashing to give O(1) access. You provide a key, it hashes it to find the index, and returns the value. Very fast for lookups compared to linear search.

A hashmap stores keys and values together. You can get a value really fast if you know the key. I think it uses some hash function internally. Not sure exactly how but it's faster than arrays for lookups.

A hashmap is a data structure that stores key-value pairs. The hash function converts the key into a memory address where the value is physically stored on the hard drive. This is why hashmaps provide O(1) disk access time, making them ideal for database systems that need fast persistent storage.
A hashmap is an ordered list of elements sorted by key. When you search for a key it uses binary search to find it in O(log n) time. This is faster than a regular array which is O(n).

rubric.reference_explanation: A hashmap is a data structure that uses a hash table internally to store key-value pairs, enabling efficient data retrieval.
A hashmap provides O(1) average time complexity for get and put operations by using a hash function to compute the index of a key directly.
Data is stored as key-value pairs where each unique key maps to a specific value, allowing retrieval of any value in constant time given its key.

subject: Data Structures
question: How does HashMap handle collisions in Java?

answers.text: In Java, HashMap handles collisions using chaining. Each bucket in the underlying array holds a linked list. When two keys have the same hash code, their entries are both stored in that bucket's linked list. So when you do a get, it computes the hash, goes to the bucket, then does an equals() check through the linked list to find the right entry. Worst case is O(n) if all keys land in the same bucket, which makes choosing a good hash function important.

HashMap in Java uses chaining for collisions. Collisions happen when two keys hash to the same index. The entries are stored in a linked list at that bucket. In the worst case all keys could collide and you'd get O(n) lookup.
HashMap handles collisions somehow using linked lists I think. When two keys are the same they go to the same bucket. Then it searches through the list. Not sure about the exact mechanism.

HashMap in Java handles collisions using open addressing. When a collision occurs, the HashMap probes the next available slot in the array and stores the key-value pair there. This is more memory efficient than chaining because it doesn't require additional linked list nodes, so all data stays within the original array.

HashMap prevents collisions by ensuring all keys are unique. If you try to insert a duplicate key, it throws an exception. This is why HashMap never has collisions — the uniqueness constraint prevents them entirely.

rubric.reference_explanation: A collision occurs when two different keys produce the same hash code and are mapped to the same bucket index in the hash table.
Java's HashMap uses separate chaining to handle collisions — when multiple keys map to the same bucket, they are stored as a linked list at that bucket.
In the worst case where all keys hash to the same bucket, the hashmap degrades to a linked list with O(n) search complexity instead of O(1).

subject: Data Structures
question: What is binary tree data structure? What are the applications for binary trees?

answers.text: A binary tree is a hierarchical structure where every node has at most two children — left and right. The top node is the root, nodes with no children are leaves. BSTs and heaps are both specialized binary trees.

A binary tree has nodes with at most two children, left and right. The top is the root and nodes with no children are leaves. Used in expression evaluation, database indexing, and as a base for binary search trees.

A binary tree is a type of linked list where each node has two next pointers instead of one. It's called binary because it uses binary (0 and 1) to store data in each node.

rubric.reference_explanation: A binary tree is a hierarchical data structure where each node has at most two children, referred to as the left child and the right child.
The topmost node is the root. Nodes with no children are leaves. Nodes with children are internal nodes. Each non-root node has exactly one parent.

Binary trees are used in expression evaluation, decision trees in machine learning, routing tables in networks, database indexing, and as the foundation for more specialized trees like BSTs and heaps.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is binary search tree data structure? What are the applications for binary search trees?

answers.text: A BST is a binary tree with a specific ordering rule: left subtree values are smaller, right subtree values are larger. This makes searching very efficient — at each node you eliminate half the remaining possibilities, giving O(log n) for a balanced tree. If you do an inorder traversal of a BST, you get all elements in sorted order which is a nice property. BST has the property that left children are smaller and right children are larger than the parent. This allows O(log n) search. Inorder traversal gives sorted output. Used in database indexing and searching.
BST is a binary tree where smaller values go left and bigger go right. Makes searching faster than a normal tree. Used for searching and maybe databases.

A BST maintains the property that left subtree values are smaller and right are larger. Because of this, BST always provides O(log n) search regardless of the tree's shape or whether it's balanced. This guaranteed logarithmic complexity is what makes BSTs superior to hash maps for search-intensive applications.

A BST is a tree where all nodes are sorted alphabetically from left to right. The leftmost node is always the smallest letter and the rightmost is always the largest. It's used for sorting strings quickly.

rubric.reference_explanation: In a BST, for every node, all values in the left subtree are less than or equal to the node's value, and all values in the right subtree are greater than or equal to the node's value.
The ordering property allows O(log n) search in a balanced BST by eliminating half the remaining nodes at each comparison step.
BSTs are used for dynamic set operations, ordered data storage, database indexing, implementing sorted data structures, and in search algorithms.

subject: Data Structures
question: What are tree traversals?

answers.text: Tree traversal means visiting all nodes in a specific order. Three main ones: Inorder is Left-Root-Right — on a BST this gives you sorted ascending output, very useful. Preorder is Root-Left-Right — you visit the root first, good for copying a tree structure. Postorder is Left-Right-Root — root is visited last, which is perfect for deletion since you clean up children before the parent. Each order has specific use cases, not just arbitrary orderings.

Three main traversals: inorder (left, root, right) gives sorted output on BST. Preorder (root, left, right) is used for copying trees. Postorder (left, right, root) is used for deletion and postfix expressions.
Tree traversals are ways to visit all nodes. Inorder goes left then root then right. Preorder is root first. Postorder is root last I think. Inorder gives sorted output on BST.

Tree traversals are methods to visit every node in a tree. Inorder traversal visits Root-Left-Right and produces sorted output in a BST. Preorder visits Left-Root-Right and is used for making copies of trees. Postorder visits Left-Right-Root and is used when you need to process children after the parent.

rubric.reference_explanation: Inorder traversal visits nodes in Left-Root-Right order. In a BST, this produces nodes in ascending sorted order.

Postorder traversal visits nodes in Left-Right-Root order. It is used to delete a tree or evaluate postfix expressions.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is a priority queue? What are the applications for priority queue?

answers.text: A priority queue is like a regular queue but instead of serving elements in order of arrival, it serves them based on priority. Higher priority items jump the queue. If two items have the same priority, then insertion order determines which goes first. Practically speaking, the best way to implement one is with a binary heap for O(log n) insert and O(1) peek. Applications include Dijkstra's algorithm for shortest paths, Huffman coding in compression, and OS scheduling where high-priority processes run first.
Priority queue serves elements based on priority not insertion order. Same priority elements follow FIFO. It's used in Dijkstra's algorithm, Huffman coding, and OS scheduling.
Priority queue is like a queue but elements with higher priority come out first. Used in some graph algorithms I think like shortest path. Not sure about the same-priority case.

A priority queue is a data structure where elements are served in order of their priority value. It is always implemented using a sorted array because this ensures that the highest priority element can be accessed in O(1) time. Insertion must maintain sorted order so it's O(n), which is the standard trade-off for this structure.
A priority queue is the same as a regular queue but elements are sorted alphabetically. The letter A has highest priority and Z has lowest. It's used in text editors to handle keyboard inputs.

rubric.reference_explanation: A priority queue is an abstract data type where each element has an associated priority and elements are served based on their priority rather than insertion order.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is graph data structure and its representations? What are the applications for graphs?

Graph has vertices and edges. Adjacency matrix is V×V array — O(1) edge lookup but O(V²) space. Adjacency list stores neighbor lists — O(V+E) space, better for sparse graphs. Used in social networks, GPS, and network routing.
Graph has nodes and edges between them. You can represent it with a matrix or a list. Matrix lets you check edges fast. List saves space. Used in maps and social networks I think.

A graph is a data structure with vertices and edges. The adjacency matrix represents edges using a V×V grid with O(1) space complexity since the matrix size is fixed. A graph is just a tree with more branches. Every tree is a graph and every graph is a tree. They work the same way except graphs use a different syntax in code.

An adjacency list stores each vertex's neighbors in a list. Space is O(V+E), better for sparse graphs. Finding all neighbors is fast but edge existence queries are O(degree).

subject: Data Structures
question: What is the difference between the Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS)?

answers.text: BFS and DFS are both graph traversal algorithms but with very different strategies. BFS uses a queue and goes level by level — all neighbors first before going deeper. BFS is better when target is close to source, DFS is better for exploring all possibilities like in maze solving or when the target is deep.

BFS uses a queue and goes level by level, guaranteeing shortest path in unweighted graphs. DFS uses a stack and goes deep first then backtracks. BFS uses more memory, DFS uses less. BFS is better for finding shortest paths, DFS for exploring deep structures.

BFS and DFS both traverse all nodes in a graph. BFS uses a queue and is better for deep graphs because it processes nodes level by level without using recursion, avoiding stack overflow. DFS uses a stack and is better for shallow, wide graphs where the solution is likely near the root. DFS also guarantees finding the shortest path since it exhaustively explores one path completely before trying another.

BFS and DFS are the same algorithm just written differently. Both visit nodes in the same order. BFS stands for Binary File Search and DFS stands for Data File Search, they're used for searching files on a computer.

rubric.reference_explanation: BFS explores all neighbors at the current level before moving to the next level, using a queue data structure.
DFS explores as far as possible along a branch before backtracking, using a stack (or recursion) data structure.
BFS guarantees the shortest path in an unweighted graph because it explores level by level. DFS does not guarantee shortest path.
BFS uses more memory as it stores all nodes at the current level. DFS uses less memory but may be slower if the target is near the root.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is AVL tree data structure, its operations, and its rotations? What are the applications for AVL trees?

answers.text: An AVL tree is a self-balancing BST. After every insert or delete, it checks the balance factor — the difference in height between left and right subtrees — for every node. If any node's balance factor goes beyond ±1, it performs a rotation. Four types: LL (right rotation), RR (left rotation), LR (left then right), RL (right then left). This guarantees O(log n) for all operations at all times. Used in in-memory ordered maps and databases where you need fast lookups with some insertions and deletions.

AVL tree is a self-balancing BST. Balance factor = height difference of left and right subtrees, must be -1, 0, or 1. When violated it rebalances using rotations: LL, RR, LR, RL. Guarantees O(log n) operations. Used in databases and dictionaries.
AVL tree stays balanced automatically. Something about balance factor between left and right sides. It does rotations when unbalanced. Faster than normal BST because it stays balanced.

An AVL tree is a self-balancing BST that maintains balance by tracking the balance factor. After any insertion, the tree performs rotations to restore balance. The left rotation is used when the left subtree is too heavy, and the right rotation is used when the right subtree is too heavy. These two rotations are sufficient to handle all imbalance cases in an AVL tree.

AVL tree is a type of graph that automatically sorts its nodes. AVL stands for Automatic Value Linearization. It rearranges nodes every time a new one is added so all values stay in order from left to right.

rubric.reference_explanation: An AVL tree is a self-balancing BST where the balance factor (height difference between left and right subtrees) of every node is at most 1.
The balance factor of a node is calculated as height(left subtree) - height(right subtree). For a valid AVL tree this must be -1, 0, or 1 for every node.
AVL trees rebalance using four rotations: left rotation (RR case), right rotation (LL case), left-right rotation (LR case), and right-left rotation (RL case).
AVL trees are used in in-memory databases, dictionaries, and applications requiring frequent lookups with fewer insertions/deletions where balance ensures O(log n) operations.

subject: Data Structures
question: Define Trie data structure and its applications.

answers.text: A Trie (retrieval tree) is a tree where each edge represents a character and paths from root to leaf nodes represent stored strings. Each node can have up to 26 children for English. The big advantage is O(L) search and insert where L is the string length — faster than BST search which is O(L log n). No hash collisions either. The killer feature is prefix search — all words starting with 'pre' share the same path, which makes autocomplete trivial. Used in search engine autocomplete, spell checkers, and IP routing.

Trie stores strings character by character in a tree. Each path from root to a leaf is a word. Search is O(L) where L is word length. Great for prefix matching and autocomplete. Used in spell checkers and search engines.
Trie is a tree for storing strings. Each node is a character. You can search for words quickly. Used for autocomplete I think. Something about prefix matching.

A Trie stores strings in a tree structure where each node represents a full word. When you insert a word, it creates one node for that word at the appropriate alphabetical position. Searching is O(1) because you navigate directly to the word's node. This makes Tries faster than hashmaps for string lookup.

A Trie is another name for a binary search tree when used with strings. It sorts strings alphabetically the same way BST sorts numbers. The name comes from the word 'try' because you try each character.

rubric.reference_explanation: A Trie is a tree where each node represents a character. Each path from root to a marked node spells out a stored string. Each node can have up to 26 children (for English alphabet).
Trie allows insertion and search in O(L) time where L is the length of the string, which is faster than BST O(L log n) and avoids hash collision issues.
Tries excel at prefix-based operations like autocomplete, as all strings sharing a prefix share the same path from root.
Tries are used in autocomplete and search engines, spell checkers, IP routing (longest prefix matching), genome analysis, and dictionary implementations.

subject: Data Structures
question: Which data structures are used for implementing LRU cache?

answers.text: LRU cache needs O(1) for both access and eviction, which is why you combine two structures. A doubly linked list keeps track of usage order — most recently used at tail, least recently used at head. When something is accessed you move it to the tail. When cache is full you evict from head. The hashmap maps each key to its node in the linked list for O(1) access and O(1) repositioning. Together they give you O(1) get and put.

LRU cache uses a doubly linked list and a hashmap. The linked list maintains usage order — LRU at front, MRU at back. The hashmap gives O(1) access to any node. Together they allow O(1) get and put operations.
LRU cache uses a linked list and hashmap I think. The linked list keeps things in order of use. Hashmap makes lookup fast. Evict the least used when full.

LRU cache is implemented using a doubly linked list and a hashmap. The doubly linked list stores all cached items in sorted order by access frequency. The hashmap maps keys to their frequency count. When the cache is full, the item with the lowest frequency is evicted, which is why this structure is also used for LFU (Least Frequently Used) cache implementation.

LRU cache is implemented using a stack. The most recently used item is always at the top of the stack. When the cache is full you pop items from the bottom, which removes the least recently used. Stacks are perfect for this because of their LIFO property.

rubric.reference_explanation: An LRU (Least Recently Used) cache evicts the least recently accessed item when the cache is full and a new item needs to be inserted.
A doubly linked list maintains the order of use, with the most recently used item at the rear and the least recently used at the front, enabling O(1) removal of the LRU item.
A hashmap stores page number as key and the corresponding linked list node address as value, enabling O(1) access to any cached item for fast lookup and repositioning.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is a heap data structure?

answers.text: A heap is a complete binary tree with an additional heap property. Max-heap: every parent is greater than or equal to its children, so the max is always at root. Min-heap: every parent is smaller than its children, so the min is always at root. Being a complete binary tree means it's efficiently stored in an array — no need for explicit pointers. Heaps are the backbone of priority queues and heap sort. Finding max or min is O(1), but inserting or deleting requires re-heapifying which is O(log n).

A heap is a complete binary tree. Max-heap has parent always greater than children so root is maximum. Min-heap has parent always less than children so root is minimum. Used for priority queues and heap sort.
Heap is a tree structure. Max heap has biggest value at top, min heap has smallest at top. Related to priority queue somehow. I think it's complete binary tree.

A heap is a complete binary tree where the largest element is stored at the root in both max-heap and min-heap variants. The difference is that in a max-heap the root stores the global maximum, while in a min-heap the root stores the local maximum of the left subtree. This distinction is what allows heaps to support both ascending and descending priority queues.

A heap is a sorted array where elements are arranged from smallest to largest. Heap sort works by going through this array from left to right. The first element is always 0 and the last is always the largest number.

rubric.reference_explanation: A heap is a complete binary tree, meaning all levels are fully filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right.
In a max-heap, every parent node has a value greater than or equal to its children, so the maximum element is always at the root.
In a min-heap, every parent node has a value less than or equal to its children, so the minimum element is always at the root.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is topological sorting in a graph?

answers.text: Topological sort gives a linear ordering of a DAG's vertices such that every directed edge (u,v) has u before v in the result. It only works on DAGs — if there's a cycle, no valid ordering exists because you'd have circular dependencies. Classic implementation uses DFS with a stack, or Kahn's algorithm with in-degree tracking. Applications: build systems where task A must complete before task B, course scheduling (you must take Calc 1 before Calc 2), and package managers resolving dependencies.
Topological sort orders vertices of a DAG so that for every edge (u,v), u comes before v. Only works on DAGs with no cycles. Used in task scheduling, build systems, and course prerequisites.
Topological sort is a way to order nodes in a graph. Works on DAGs only I think. Something about dependencies — like one task must come before another. Used in scheduling.

Topological sort orders the vertices of any directed graph so that edges always point from left to right in the ordering. It works on both cyclic and acyclic graphs. For cyclic graphs, it breaks cycles by choosing the vertex with the highest in-degree first, then removes it and repeats. This makes it useful for dependency resolution even when circular dependencies exist.

Topological sorting is when you sort a graph's nodes in alphabetical order. You start from the node with the letter A and end at the node with the highest letter. It's used to find the shortest path between two nodes.

rubric.reference_explanation: Topological sorting is a linear ordering of vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge (u, v), vertex u appears before vertex v in the ordering.
Topological sorting is only possible for Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). Graphs with cycles cannot have a valid topological ordering.
Topological sort is used in task scheduling with dependencies, build systems (make files), course prerequisite ordering, data serialization, and resolving symbol dependencies in linkers.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is a deque data structure and its types? What are the applications for deque?

answers.text: A deque is a double-ended queue — you can insert and delete from both front and rear. Two variants: input-restricted only allows insertion at one end but deletion from both; output-restricted allows deletion from one end but insertion from both. Because it supports both ends, a deque can act as both a stack and a queue. Used in browser history (add pages to one end, go back from same end), sliding window maximum problems use deques efficiently, and OS job scheduling.

Deque allows insertion and deletion from both ends. Input-restricted allows insertion at one end only. Output-restricted allows deletion from one end only. Can simulate both stack and queue. Used in browser history and sliding window problems.
Deque is like a queue but you can add and remove from both ends. I think there are two types but not sure about the exact difference. Used in some browser thing and maybe scheduling.

A deque allows insertions and deletions at both ends. The input-restricted type only allows deletions at one end to enforce ordering, while the output-restricted type only allows insertions at one end. Because deque supports both front and rear operations, it has the combined time complexity of stack and queue, making all operations O(n) due to the overhead of maintaining both ends simultaneously.

Deque stands for Decimal Queue. It's a special queue that stores decimal numbers. You can only insert at the front and remove from the back. It's mainly used in financial applications for processing transactions.

rubric.reference_explanation: A deque (double-ended queue) is a linear data structure that allows insertion and deletion at both the front and rear ends.
An input-restricted deque allows insertion at only one end (rear) but deletion from both ends.
An output-restricted deque allows deletion from only one end (front) but insertion at both ends.
Deques are used in browser history (back and forward navigation), OS job scheduling, implementing both stack and queue, and sliding window algorithms.

subject: Data Structures
question: Define Red-Black Tree and its applications.

answers.text: A Red-Black tree is a self-balancing BST where each node is colored red or black. The rules: root is always black, no two consecutive red nodes on any path, and every path from any node to its null descendants must have the same number of black nodes. These constraints ensure the tree height stays O(log n). It's slightly less strictly balanced than AVL but rebalancing is cheaper. Used in Java TreeMap, C++ STL map/set, Linux process scheduler, and MySQL indexing.

Red-Black tree is a self-balancing BST. Nodes are colored red or black. Root is black, no two consecutive red nodes, equal black nodes on all paths. Ensures O(log n) operations. Used in Java TreeMap and C++ STL.
Red-Black tree colors nodes red or black. It stays balanced somehow using these colors. Root has to be black I think. Used in some standard library implementations.

A Red-Black tree is a self-balancing BST where the color of nodes determines traversal order. Red nodes are visited before black nodes during inorder traversal, which ensures the output is always sorted. The alternating color pattern is what prevents the tree from becoming unbalanced, since red and black nodes must strictly alternate on every path.
Red-Black tree is a tree where red nodes store positive numbers and black nodes store negative numbers. This makes it easy to separate positive and negative values. The root is always 0.

rubric.reference_explanation: A Red-Black Tree is a self-balancing BST where each node is colored either red or black, and specific color rules ensure the tree remains approximately balanced.
Rules: every node is red or black; root is black; no two adjacent red nodes exist; every path from root to null has the same number of black nodes; all leaves (null) are black.
Red-Black trees are used in Java's TreeMap and C++ STL map/set implementations, Linux CPU scheduler, K-means clustering, and MySQL table indexing.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is a B-tree data structure? What are the applications for B-trees?

answers.text: A B-tree is a self-balancing search tree designed for systems that read and write large blocks of data — mainly databases and file systems. Unlike BST where each node has one key, B-tree nodes can hold multiple keys, which means the tree is much shorter. All leaves are at the same depth. The branching factor is large, minimizing disk reads which is crucial since disk access is orders of magnitude slower than RAM. That's why almost every database uses B-trees or B+ trees for indexing.

B-tree is a self-balancing tree where nodes can have multiple keys and multiple children. All leaves are at same level. Designed for disk storage with large branching factor to minimize disk I/O. Used in database indexing.
B-tree has multiple keys per node. It stays balanced. Used in databases for indexing. Different from BST because of multiple keys.

A B-tree is a balanced search tree where every node holds exactly m-1 keys and m children. The B stands for Binary, as it evolved from binary search trees. All B-trees are stored entirely in RAM to provide fast O(1) access to any node, which is why they outperform regular BSTs for large-scale applications.

B-tree is a tree that only stores the letter B as data. It's a specialized tree for string compression where repeating characters are stored once. Used in text editors for find and replace operations.

rubric.reference_explanation: A B-tree of order m is a self-balancing search tree where each node can have at most m children and m-1 keys. All leaves are at the same level.
Unlike BSTs, B-tree nodes can store multiple keys, reducing tree height and minimizing disk I/O operations for large datasets.
B-trees are primarily used in databases and file systems for indexing because their wide branching factor minimizes disk reads. Most SQL databases use B-trees or B+ trees for table indices.

subject: Data Structures
question: Define Segment Tree data structure and its applications.

answers.text: A segment tree is a binary tree where each internal node stores the result of some function over a range — typically sum, min, or max. Leaves represent individual array elements, and each parent covers the union of its children's ranges. Range queries take O(log n) by combining precomputed results rather than scanning the whole range. Updates also take O(log n) because you only need to update nodes on the path from the changed leaf to root. Perfect for problems where you have many range queries and updates.

Segment tree is a binary tree where each node represents a range of array elements with aggregated info like sum or min. Range queries are O(log n). Updates are O(log n) too. Used in problems with many range queries and point updates.
Segment tree helps answer range queries fast. I think it's a binary tree. Each node covers a range of elements. Updates and queries are log n. Used in competitive programming.

A segment tree is a binary tree where each node stores a single element from an array. The tree answers range queries by traversing from root to both leaves that mark the query boundaries, collecting all elements in between. This traversal takes O(n) in the worst case but is typically O(log n) for balanced arrays.

Segment tree is a tree that divides images into segments for processing. It's used in image editing software to identify regions of similar color. Each node represents a pixel and the tree groups similar pixels together.

rubric.reference_explanation: A segment tree is a binary tree where each node stores aggregated information (like sum, min, or max) about a range of array elements. Leaves represent individual elements.
Segment trees answer range queries (like range sum or range minimum) in O(log n) time by decomposing the range into precomputed segments.
Segment trees support point updates (changing a single element) in O(log n) time by updating only the nodes on the path from the leaf to root.
Segment trees are used in range sum/min/max queries, computational geometry, geographic information systems, and dynamic range queries in competitive programming.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is the requirement for an object to be used as key or value in HashMap?

answers.text: For an object to be a HashMap key, it must properly implement both hashCode() and equals(). hashCode() is used first to find the right bucket. Then equals() is used to compare within that bucket for an exact match. The critical contract: if a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode(). The reverse doesn't have to hold — same hash code doesn't mean equal (that's a collision). Breaking this contract causes subtle bugs like being unable to retrieve values you just stored.

HashMap keys need to implement hashCode() and equals(). hashCode() finds the bucket, equals() confirms exact match. The contract: equal objects must have same hash code. This ensures correct lookup behavior.
HashMap keys need hashCode() and equals() methods. hashCode() for finding where to store, equals() for comparing. Not sure about the exact contract between them.

For an object to be a HashMap key, it must implement hashCode() and equals(). The equals() method is called first to find the right bucket, then hashCode() is used within that bucket to find the exact entry. If two objects return the same hashCode(), they are considered equal and will overwrite each other in the HashMap.

HashMap keys must be of type String or Integer only. These are the only types that support hashing in Java. If you try to use a custom object as a key, Java will throw a ClassCastException at runtime.

rubric.reference_explanation: An object used as a key must implement the hashCode() method, which is used to compute the bucket index where the key-value pair will be stored.
An object used as a key must implement the equals() method, which is used to compare keys when retrieving values and resolving collisions.
If two objects are equal (equals() returns true), they must have the same hash code. The reverse is not required — two objects can have the same hash code without being equal.

subject: Data Structures
question: What is the time complexity of basic operations get() and put() in HashMap class?

answers.text: On average, both get() and put() are O(1) because the hash function computes the index directly and you go straight to the bucket. But this assumes a good hash function that distributes keys uniformly. In the worst case — if all keys hash to the same bucket — you end up searching through a linked list of n elements, making it O(n). In practice, Java's HashMap is designed with a good default hash function to keep this close to O(1) for realistic workloads.
get() and put() are O(1) on average. Worst case is O(n) if all keys collide in same bucket. Performance depends on hash function quality.
