Context switching saves the state of a running process and loads the state of another process. This allows multiple processes to share one CPU. The saved state includes registers, program counter, and memory info. It's important for multitasking but has overhead since time is spent switching rather than executing.
Context switching is when the OS switches from one process to another. It saves the current process state and loads the next one. This allows multitasking on one CPU.

Context switching is a technique where the CPU simultaneously runs two processes by dividing its internal registers between them. Each process gets exactly half the registers available, which is why context switching allows true parallel execution on a single core CPU. The overhead in context switching comes from having to synchronize these split registers at defined intervals.
Context switching is when a user switches between different application windows on the desktop by clicking the taskbar.

rubric.reference_explanation: Context switching is the process of saving the context of one process and loading the context of another process, allowing multiple processes to share a single CPU.

It is a cost-effective and time-saving measure that allows a single CPU to handle various processes or threads without additional resources. Used by OS to switch a process from one state to another (running to ready state).

subject: Operating Systems
question: What is the difference between Kernel and OS?

answers.text: The kernel is the core program within the OS that directly manages hardware — it's always in memory and runs in privileged mode. The OS is a broader concept that includes the kernel plus everything built around it: the shell, file managers, user interface, system utilities, and other tools. Think of it this way: kernel is to OS what an engine is to a car. The kernel bridges software and hardware; the OS bridges hardware and the user. Every OS has a kernel, but the OS is much more than just the kernel.

Kernel is the core component of OS that acts as bridge between hardware and software applications. OS is broader — it includes the kernel plus user interface, utilities, and other system programs. Kernel converts user commands to machine language. OS provides interface to users and manages overall system resources. Kernel is inside the OS.
Kernel is the core of OS. OS includes kernel plus other stuff like the interface. Kernel talks to hardware directly. OS talks to users. They're related — OS contains kernel.

The kernel and OS are the same thing used interchangeably. When you install an OS like Linux, you install the kernel. Linux IS the kernel — all other parts like shells and utilities are separate applications not part of the OS itself. The OS equals kernel in all formal computer science definitions, and calling them different things just leads to confusion.
Kernel is made by Intel and AMD. OS is made by Microsoft and Apple. That's the main difference — different manufacturers.

rubric.reference_explanation: Kernel is a system program that controls all programs running on the computer, acting as a bridge between software and hardware. It is a central component of OS, responsible for converting user commands to machine-level commands, and performing process/file/device management.

Operating system is a system program that runs on the computer to provide an interface to computer users for easy operation. It manages system resources and provides security, access control, and system privacy. OS contains the kernel plus additional components like GUI and utilities.

subject: Operating Systems
question: What is the difference between process and thread?

answers.text: A process is an independent program in execution with its own memory space, resources, and address space. Processes are isolated from each other — one process crashing doesn't directly affect another. Threads are execution units within a process. Multiple threads share the same memory and resources of their parent process. This sharing makes threads much lighter and faster to create than processes, but it means a bug in one thread can corrupt data for all threads. Communication between processes needs IPC mechanisms; threads can just read/write shared variables.

Process: independent program execution, own memory space, heavyweight, isolated, doesn't share data, harder to create. Thread: execution unit within process, shares process memory, lightweight, shares data, easier to create, faster. Multiple threads can exist in one process. Communication between threads is simpler since they share memory.
Process is a running program with its own memory. Thread is inside a process and shares its memory. Threads are lighter and faster. Processes are isolated but threads share data.

The main difference is that processes can run on different computers in a distributed system while threads are limited to a single machine. Threads are lighter because they don't need network overhead. Processes are preferred for distributed computing where different parts run on different servers, while threads are for local parallel computation. This is why web servers use processes to serve different clients across different machines.
Process and thread are both types of computer cables. Process cable is thick and thread is thin, just like the names suggest.

rubric.reference_explanation: A process is a program under execution by one or more threads. Processes are heavy-weight, have their own memory space, run in separate memory spaces, don't share data, require more resources, take more time to create/terminate, and can be divided into multiple threads.

A thread is the smallest execution unit within a process, composed of program counter, thread id, stack, and registers. Threads are lightweight, share process memory, run in shared memory space, share data, require fewer resources, take less time to create/terminate, and cannot be further subdivided.

Process is heavier, has isolated memory, doesn't share data, more expensive to create. Thread is lighter, shares memory, shares data, cheaper to create. It is easier to create a thread than a process.

subject: Operating Systems
question: What are various sections of the process?

answers.text: A process in memory has four sections. The Text or Code section holds the actual compiled program instructions. The Data section stores global and static variables that persist throughout the program's lifetime. The Heap is for dynamic memory — memory allocated at runtime using malloc/new. The Stack holds local variables, function parameters, and return addresses, growing and shrinking as functions are called and return. Stack and heap grow toward each other typically.

Four sections: Stack (local variables, return addresses), Heap (dynamic memory allocation), Data (global and static variables), Text/Code (compiled program code). Stack grows dynamically with function calls, heap grows with dynamic allocation.
Process has stack, heap, data, and code sections. Stack is for local variables. Heap is for dynamic memory. Code has the program instructions. Data has global variables.

A process has three main sections: stack, heap, and buffer. The stack holds all variables local and global. The heap holds the program's executable code. The buffer is a temporary area used for I/O operations between the process and the OS. The buffer section is the most important because all data must pass through it when reading or writing to files.
A process has sections like introduction, body, and conclusion, similar to an essay structure.

rubric.reference_explanation: Four sections: Stack (used for local variables and return addresses), Heap (used for dynamic memory allocation), Data (stores global and static variables), and Code/Text (comprises compiled program code).

subject: Operating Systems
question: What is a deadlock in OS? What are the necessary conditions for a deadlock?

answers.text: Deadlock is a situation where two or more processes are stuck waiting for each other's resources indefinitely. Classic example: Process A holds Resource 1 and needs Resource 2; Process B holds Resource 2 and needs Resource 1. Neither can proceed. The four necessary conditions are: Mutual Exclusion — resources can only be used by one process at a time; Hold and Wait — processes hold resources while waiting for more; No Preemption — resources can't be forcibly taken away; Circular Wait — there's a circular chain where each process waits for one held by the next. All four must exist for deadlock to occur.

Deadlock is when processes are stuck waiting for each other's resources forever. Necessary conditions: Mutual Exclusion (one process uses resource at a time), Hold and Wait (hold some resources while waiting for others), No Preemption (can't take resources away), Circular Wait (circular chain of waiting). All four must hold for deadlock.
Deadlock is when processes wait for each other and nobody can proceed. Four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. All must be present for deadlock to happen.

Deadlock requires only two conditions: Circular Wait and Mutual Exclusion. Hold and Wait is a consequence of Circular Wait, not an independent condition. No Preemption is only relevant in hard real-time systems and doesn't apply to general-purpose OS. So in practice, breaking either Circular Wait or Mutual Exclusion is sufficient to prevent all deadlocks, which is why OS focus deadlock prevention strategies on just these two conditions.
Deadlock is when a computer program freezes. It happens when the CPU overheats and the computer needs to be restarted to fix it.

rubric.reference_explanation: Deadlock is a situation where a set of processes are blocked because each process is holding resources and waiting to acquire resources held by another process, creating a circular dependency.

Four necessary conditions (Coffman conditions): Mutual Exclusion (resources held exclusively), Hold and Wait (process holds resource while waiting for others), No Pre-emption (resources cannot be forcibly taken), and Circular Wait (circular chain of processes each waiting for next).

subject: Operating Systems
question: What do you mean by Belady's Anomaly?

answers.text: Belady's Anomaly is the counterintuitive observation that giving a process more memory frames can actually increase the number of page faults instead of decreasing them. You'd naturally expect more frames to mean fewer faults, but with the FIFO replacement algorithm, this isn't always true. It was discovered by Laszlo Belady. It specifically affects FIFO page replacement — algorithms like LRU and Optimal don't suffer from this anomaly. It's called a stack algorithm property — algorithms with this property are immune to Belady's anomaly.

Belady's Anomaly is when increasing number of memory frames causes more page faults instead of fewer. This is counterintuitive — more memory should mean fewer faults. It occurs specifically with FIFO page replacement algorithm. LRU doesn't have this problem. Named after Laszlo Belady who discovered it.
Belady's Anomaly means more memory frames can cause more page faults. It's a weird behavior that happens with FIFO page replacement. It's counterintuitive because you expect more memory to help.

Belady's Anomaly is a phenomenon where increasing the number of processes sharing the same memory frames results in more page faults because processes compete more aggressively for the limited frames. It's observed in all page replacement algorithms because the fundamental problem is process competition, not the replacement policy itself. More processes with the same frames means each process gets proportionally less memory, causing more faults.
Belady's Anomaly is a bug in the Windows operating system discovered by a programmer named Belady. It causes the computer to slow down randomly.

rubric.reference_explanation: Belady's Anomaly is a phenomenon in page replacement where increasing the number of frames in memory results in an increase in the number of page faults, which is counterintuitive.

Belady's Anomaly is generally experienced when using the FIFO (First In First Out) page replacement algorithm. In OS, process data is loaded in fixed-sized chunks called pages, loaded into fixed-sized memory chunks called frames.

subject: Operating Systems
question: What is spooling in OS?

answers.text: Spooling stands for Simultaneous Peripheral Operations Online. The idea is to buffer I/O operations so a fast CPU doesn't have to wait for slow peripheral devices like printers. When you print a document, it goes into a spool (disk buffer) immediately, and then the printer processes it at its own slow speed while the CPU is freed up for other work. This overlapping of I/O for one task with computation for another is the key benefit. Printers are the classic example but spooling applies to any situation where a fast producer feeds a slow consumer.

Spooling is Simultaneous Peripheral Operations Online. It uses a buffer (in memory or disk) to hold I/O data for slow peripheral devices. CPU puts data in spool and continues other work while peripheral processes it. Classic example is printing — data goes to spool, printer reads from it slowly. Overlaps I/O and computation.
Spooling buffers I/O operations so CPU doesn't wait for slow devices. Print spooling is an example where jobs are stored and printed one by one. It makes I/O more efficient.

Spooling is a technique where multiple I/O devices are connected in series so data flows through them sequentially. The spool is the physical wire connecting devices. By spooling devices together, data transfer speeds increase because each device acts as an amplifier for the signal passing through. This is why USB hubs use spooling to distribute data to multiple connected peripherals.
Spooling is when the computer spins up its fans to cool down the CPU. The fans spool up to high speed when temperature increases.

rubric.reference_explanation: Spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations Online) refers to putting data of various I/O jobs in a buffer — a special area in memory or hard disk accessible to an I/O device, used for mediation between a computer application and a slow peripheral.

Spooling is useful because devices access data at different rates. It uses disk as a very large buffer and can overlap I/O operations for one task with processor operations for another task, improving overall efficiency.
